note: Draft data for Anoria's Places as each player's own stack. No pictures. 'pic': the Place has a picture today. 'pw0': the rule the Place has in the game today, where the draft changes it. 'sure': how sure the sentence is (3 well attested, 2 the usual account, 1 tradition or legend, and the sentence says so). 'll' is [longitude, latitude].

COM.gave: Money. Whoever held the market was paid by everyone who used it.

IND.gave: Made things: ships, arms, books and tools, for less than anyone else could make them.

IDE.gave: Knowledge, and teachers whose students carried it on.

LAND.gave: Ground nobody could be pushed off.

CUL.gave: Fame. People came, watched, believed and remembered.

LAW.gave: Order. What was decided there held everywhere else.

ROU.gave: Reach. Whoever held the way could be anywhere first.

spark.tx: At an Outpost or the Crossroads, whoever holds it gets 1 more Spark next turn.

cheap.tx: At an Outpost or the Crossroads, Figures arriving here cost 1 less.

forge.tx: Whoever holds it pays 1 less for Relics and Deeds.

arms.tx: A Figure has +1 Might on the turn it arrives here.

draw.tx: Whoever holds it draws a card each round.

line.tx: A Legacy Line made by a Figure arriving here scores 1 more Renown.

closed.tx: At a Gate or an Outpost, only the player whose side it is on can walk Figures in.

narrow.tx: Each player can have no more than two Figures here.

crowd.tx: It scores 2 Renown, not 1, for a player who holds it with two or more Figures.

arena.tx: Winning a clash here scores 1 Renown.

seal.tx: While you hold it, your last Seal cannot be broken.

sanctuary.tx: Figures here can't be targeted by the other player's Deeds.

link.tx: It is linked to every Place.

road.tx: A Figure that arrives here can walk on the same turn.

places.fact: It was a web of caravan routes linking China and the Mediterranean, and the cities along it grew rich and powerful on what passed through.
Bartolomeu Dias rounded it in 1488, and the sea road it opened between Europe and Asia carried the spice trade until the Suez Canal opened in 1869.
Norse sailors built a base here to mend their ships and explore farther south, and wood they cut has been dated to the year 1021.
The northern and southern branches of the Silk Road met at this oasis, so every caravan between China and the West passed through it.
Its harbour commanded the strait between the Indian Ocean and the China seas, and a visitor in the 1510s counted 84 languages spoken in its market.
Its sultans controlled the gold trade of the East African coast and struck their own coins, and Ibn Battuta, who came in 1331, called it one of the most beautiful towns he had seen.
For some four hundred years its merchants held most of Europe's trade in spices and silk with the East.
The kings of Egypt set out to gather every book in the world here, and by one ancient account books found on ships in the harbour were taken and copied.
It was founded in 1675 to solve the problem of finding longitude at sea, and since 1884 the world's maps and clocks have been set from its meridian.
The Ming shipyards here on the Yangtze built the great ships of Zheng He's fleets from 1405, and some of their docks can still be seen.
Polynesian voyagers settled this island about eight hundred years ago, and its clans carved nearly a thousand stone moai to honour their ancestors.
Whoever holds the Rock watches the only way between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, and from 1779 it withstood a siege of more than three and a half years.
Its walls were built and rebuilt over about two thousand years to hold China's northern frontier.
In 480 BC the pass between the mountain and the sea was so narrow that a few thousand Greeks held back the Persian army here for days.
Its gates and walled paths wind like a maze to confuse an attacker, and in four hundred years it has never been destroyed by war, fire or earthquake.
Haiti built it on a mountain top after winning its freedom, with hundreds of cannon, so that France could never take the country back.
A rich strike of silver here in 483 BC paid for the two hundred warships with which Athens beat the Persians at Salamis.
Its name went on blades of patterned steel, forged from ingots brought from India, that were prized from Spain to Persia.
The kings of Kush ruled from this city on the Nile, and the great heaps of slag left by its iron furnaces can still be seen.
Rome's emperors gave the people games here to keep their favour, and it could seat around 50,000.
Every four years the Greek cities called a truce so that athletes could travel here to compete, and the winners' names were kept for more than a thousand years.
Rome built it in 312 BC to move its legions south quickly, the first of the roads that held the empire together.
In this meadow in 1215 the barons made King John put his seal to Magna Carta, which said that even the king must obey the law.
Its merchant fleets controlled the trade of the western Mediterranean, and its round harbour had sheds for some two hundred warships to guard it.
Plato taught here from about 387 BC, and Aristotle came as a student, stayed twenty years and went on to teach Alexander.
Copernicus studied here and Galileo taught here for eighteen years, and its anatomy theatre of 1595 is the oldest still standing.
Under the caliphs of Baghdad, scholars turned the books of Greece, Persia and India into Arabic and built on them.
For some seven hundred years students came from as far as China and Korea to study at this monastery, and the pilgrim Xuanzang wrote of thousands of them.
Athens spent the tribute of its allies on the temples here, to show all Greece who led it, and the Parthenon was finished in 432 BC.
It held about 3,000 people, and all London, from apprentices to lords, came to its plays.
The emperor and the nobles of Vienna competed to keep the best musicians, and Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven and Schubert all worked here within fifty years.
The popes brought the best painters in Italy to this chapel to show the glory of Rome, and Michelangelo painted its ceiling between 1508 and 1512.
Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz printed about 180 Bibles around 1455, and within fifty years presses across Europe had turned out millions of books.
Rome's Senate met beside it and its courts sat in it, and the laws made here were obeyed from Britain to Egypt.
Its gold florin, first struck in 1252, was trusted across Europe, and its bankers lent money to kings and popes.
When Rome attacked in 213 BC, the war machines Archimedes built kept its walls from being taken for about two years.
The kings of Persia received the tribute of their empire here, and its stairways are carved with the envoys of twenty-three peoples bringing gifts.
Hammurabi ruled from this city, and about 1754 BC he had his 282 laws carved on stone and set up where anyone could see them.
For five hundred years China was governed from behind its walls, and no one entered without the emperor's leave.
By Haudenosaunee tradition the Great Law of Peace was agreed here, and the council of the nations has kept its fire at Onondaga ever since.
Emperors ruled from this city for more than eleven hundred years, and Justinian's lawyers here wrote the code that much of Europe's law grew from.
Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, with craftsmen from across his empire, and it took about twenty years.
At its court a person rose by skill in poetry, music and handwriting, and Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji there about 1010.
It grew rich where the salt caravans of the Sahara met the gold boats of the Niger, and its wealth paid for its scholars and libraries.
The great market of the Aztec capital drew some sixty thousand buyers and sellers a day, by the count of the Spaniards who saw it in 1519.
The first women's rights convention in the United States met here in 1848, and its declaration that all men and women are created equal was taken up across the country.
Its kings ruled the plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo from within stone walls eleven metres high, built without mortar.
For a thousand years its kilns made porcelain for China's emperors and for buyers from Japan to Europe, who could not copy it for centuries.
People came from all over Britain to gather here at midwinter, and its builders hauled some of the stones about 150 miles from Wales.
Khufu's builders raised it so that the king would be remembered as a god, and for about 3,800 years nothing people built stood taller.
Legend sets Heorot, the hall where Beowulf fought Grendel, at Lejre in Denmark, where the remains of great timber halls of that age have been dug up.
The Nabataeans grew rich here taxing the incense caravans from Arabia, and carved their tombs into the rose-red cliffs.
The kings of Assyria ruled an empire that reached from the Nile to Iran from this city, and Ashurbanipal's library here held tens of thousands of clay tablets.
The Inca built it on a ridge high in the Andes, without mortar, wheels or iron tools, where only a few guarded paths lead in.
The Saudeleur rulers of Pohnpei built it of basalt columns on nearly a hundred artificial islets in a lagoon, and made the island's chiefs live there under their eye.
King Kashyapa built his palace on top of this rock, two hundred metres above the forest, and the way up passed between the paws of a great lion built of brick.
The Inca tied their empire together with some 40,000 kilometres of road, and relay runners carried the ruler's orders along it about 240 kilometres a day.
Ships sailed from this port down the Gulf to India and China, and it is the harbour Sinbad sets out from in the Thousand and One Nights.
For centuries the gold, salt and grain of West Africa changed hands in its market on the Niger, and its traders worked hand in hand with Timbuktu's.
The guild of bronze casters has worked for the Obas of Benin since about the 13th century, and their plaques kept the kingdom's history on the palace walls.
